en: At Wujingzhai, Zhihu Yin is neither a layman nor a monk;
he is neither an ordinary man nor an immortal. He has cleared away the thorny brambles and passed through the diamond circle.
His eyebrows are knitted together, and his nostrils reach toward the heavens. Having burned the protective talisman, it falls upon the paper like clouds and mist. Sometimes...
He thatched a hut and sat in meditation atop a desolate mountain peak; at other times, he would sleep in a tavern on the streets of Chang’an.
His spirit swallowed the nine provinces, yet his pouch held not a single coin. When the time arrived, he shed his skin like a cicada; eighty-four thousand *śarīra* relics emerged.
His praises could never be exhausted, and so he spoke this verse: "Alas! This is why he is called Ji Dian."
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Ji Dian, the Hermit of Qiandao Lake.
Compiled by Shen Mengpan of Renhe. Introduction.
Tearing asunder the net, one casts off the entanglements of craving; Entering the Golden Field, one emulates the Golden Immortal.
Hair falls with the stroke of the blade as the roots of dust are purified; Robes follow the clouds as the cranial protuberance becomes perfect.
At the moment of awakening, one departs from the sea of affliction; When concentration arises, one transcends the barrier of birth and death.
The Imperial Grace and the Buddha’s Virtue are both fully repaid; How can one flower fail to bloom as a lotus amidst the fire?
These eight lines of verse reveal that among the Three Teachings, Chan alone is most wondrous. To speak further:

during the reign of Emperor Gaozong of the Great Song, there was a *dharmakāya* arhat who, while residing on Mount Tiantai, manifested a transformation body to appear in Lin’an Prefecture. Mount Tiantai...
In Taizhou Prefecture of Eastern Zhejiang, there was an elder at Guoqing Temple named Yi Ben, whose style name was Fakong.
He was a living Buddha who had cultivated himself through successive kalpas. At that time, as the year drew to a close, thick clouds gathered and snow fell in profusion.
The elder sat alone in the abbot’s quarters, ordering the kitchen to prepare the evening meal. With the sounding of a single cloud-board, the assembly of monks gathered together.
When they reached the meditation hall after the meal was finished, the Elder remained seated upon his Zen chair in the abbot’s quarters while the attendant brought him tea.
Suddenly, a sound like a clap of thunder resounded. The Elder asked, "What was that sound?
He then proceeded with the attendant to the Dharma Hall, ascended to the Buddha Hall, and entered the Hall of Arhats, where he saw an Arhat topple over from his chair to the ground.

The Elder Yin knew [the truth], yet feigned ignorance, saying, "I shall attend to this matter separately. When the assembly arrived at the abbot’s quarters, he ordered the attendant to light incense and candles;
at that moment, the snow was falling even more heavily. A poem says:
The Realized One of Gushan feasts at the Purple Tenuity; Shuangcheng strikes and shatters the jade-glass.
The universe is so vast and clear it is difficult to distinguish; All sentient beings on the great earth are lost on the right path.
The Elder sits upright in his meditation chair, eyes closed and brows lowered. After entering samādhi for a short while, he returns and says: "I am going."
[The monks] said, "We are of dull minds and shallow understanding; we are not familiar with the subtleties of Chan. We wish to hear the details.
The Elder said, "There is no harm in speaking of it. The Purple-Footed Arhat, weary of stillness and longing for movement, has already departed for another place.
On another day, if you have someone who knows him, I, this old monk, shall wait for more than a month and go in person to entrust [the matter] to him."
With these words, the assembly dispersed. Now, let us speak of Li Maochun of Tiantai County in Taizhou Prefecture.
He was a descendant of Li Fuma from the reign of Emperor Gaozong and had served as a Zanshan in the Chongfeng Palace. Being a man of pure and generous character, he had no desire for office;
he resigned his post and lived in seclusion on Mount Tiantai. He had only one wife, Lady Wang, who was over thirty years of age and had never...
As he grew up, he frequently prayed to the gods and beseeched the Buddhas. One night, the King’s consort dreamed that she swallowed the sun;
from then on, she conceived. After ten months, she gave birth. It was the first watch of the eighth day of the twelfth month in the third year of Emperor Guangzong of the Song dynasty.
A son was born, and a crimson light filled the chamber while auspicious vapors pervaded the gate. The Court Counselor was greatly rejoiced. Gradually...

After more than a month had passed, the Elder of Guoqing Monastery came to visit. Zanshan received him, and after the tea ceremony upon ascending the hall was concluded, the Elder said, "I have recently heard that you, Excellency, have welcomed a son.
I have come specifically to offer my congratulations and would venture to request a glimpse of the child; would this be permissible? Zanshan replied, "I am honored by my Master’s generous intent;
however, as the infant has been born but a short time ago, his body is not yet pure. How could I dare to show him to you?"
“My teacher! The Elder said, “What prevents you from seeing him? Zanshan said, “My teacher, please sit for a moment,” and he immediately entered the inner quarters.
Anshi Wang was the brother-in-law of Zanshan’s wife. Zanshan said, “The Elder of Guoqing Temple wishes to see my child;
do you think it would be improper? Anshi replied, “That monk is of lofty virtue and profound character; he wishes to see this boy.”
"Do not be sparing with him, Your Honor. The Zanshan then had a maidservant carry the young monk forward.
The Elder hurriedly took him by the hand and said, "What a swift-footed child! Do not let him lose his way. The boy merely smiled slightly.

Having observed him, the Elder handed him back to the maidservant and said, "This child shall in the future penetrate both heaven and earth, entering the ranks of the sages and transcending the mundane world. I, this old monk—"
He sent one man named Xiuyuan to have him cultivate his *benming yuanchen* (original life-spirit). Zanshan rose to take his leave.

As the Elder was bidding farewell, Zanshan said, "I originally intended to leave Master Suyi behind, but since there is a meal with meat at my residence, I hope you will allow me to visit your monastery.

The Elder said, "This old monk is departing for the West in the tenth month. If you, Great Man, will not abandon me, I would be grateful if you would accompany me for a short distance. Zanshan replied:
"My teacher, your years are not yet advanced; you ought to enjoy the pure blessings of tranquility.

Having taken his leave and returned to the temple, the Zanshan (Court Gentleman) that day prepared an extensive and splendid banquet to entertain his relatives and friends, which dispersed at nightfall. Several days after the Elder returned to the temple, the time arrived for the Shangyuan Festival.
The Elder ascended the seat in the Dharma Hall, struck the drum three times, and the assembly of monks gathered like clouds, entering in single file as incense was burned.
The two ranks of officials stand in formation; the great assembly listens with pure attention.
On the fifteenth day of the first month, the flower lanterns are released; the common people everywhere rejoice in peace and prosperity.

Since this auspicious occasion of the New Year is not for formal exposition, let us return home and speak but a single word. Having returned and not coming back again, the matter of one’s own house is left to oneself.
The family knows. If one were to let others know of this, one would certainly be subjected to their criticism and gossip; therefore, by not speaking of it, one simply remains as they are.
There is no need to speculate about the matter of birth and death. This mountain monk departs for the Western Paradise on the sixteenth day (2x9);
he specifically informs all the mountains to come in succession. Who understands and awakens to the talk of birth and death? Everyone originally possesses this path. Time passes.
How many people have we overtaken? The green waters and blue mountains remain as they were. The mountain hues are blue and the water’s luster is green;
Lord Yama has no face to show. I send this word to the great assembly: practice the Way early, so that in a future life we may together ascend to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
When the Elder finished his recitation, the assembly all knelt down and said, "Our Master, we pray that you will remain for another several decades.
The Elder replied, "Death is a fixed destiny; how can it be delayed? The monks shed tears.

The Elder ordered his attendant to transcribe his Dharma words and to quickly inform the various mountain monasteries to come and escort him on the morning of the eighteenth day. On that day, the Elder descended from the Dharma seat.
The seat was prepared, and upon the completion of the construction of the shrine, the eighteenth day arrived. All the mountain monks and others gathered, and Li Zanshan also arrived.
After the midday meal, they entered the Abbot’s quarters to meet. The Elder bathed and changed his robes, then sat upright upon the meditation chair in the Anle Hall.
The abbots from various mountains and all the attendants stood to the left and right, surrounding him in a dense throng. The Elder—
The Elder called his five disciples. "Distribute the robes, bowls, and other items equally among you. The *jian-si* (superintendent) shall keep a count.
All five of you must be prudent; do not act with negligence or license. The disciples wept bitterly. The Elder said, "The time has come. Quickly burn incense and light the candles.
The assembly of monks took their leave and bowed, chanting the scriptures in unison. The Elder then ordered that [the items] be taken.
Taking up paper and brush, he then composed a quatrain:
At eighty-nine years of age, In all things, nature is empty and without flaw.
Today I cast off my hands and return to the West; I stroll at ease within the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Having finished writing, it was exactly noon. He lowered his eyes, closed his brows, and passed into parinirvāṇa. The assembly each raised their voices in lamentation and requested that the Dharma-body be placed within the coffin.
On the ninth day of the second month—already three weeks since his passing—the sky was bright and the air clear.
People from near and far arrived to escort the funeral procession. They then requested the Elder Daoqing of Jiyuan Temple to lead the way. The Elder stood...
From atop the sedan chair, he said: "Listen, all you people!
When willows are lovely and flowers are charming in the days of the second month, when silks and brocades cluster in the famous gardens—yet you, Master, do not cherish the beauty of spring;
you cast it aside and return to the West to revert to the Original Source. I respectfully venerate the National Teacher, Elder Xingkong Wuheshang.
Jue Ling: Since the fundamental nature is empty, how can there be any phenomena? Yet, alas, the Zen mind remains luminous and imperishable.
He recited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; his calligraphy was in the *kaogu* style. Taking the Buddha as his kin and springs and rocks as his friends, he lived for sixty-nine years.

There is neither beauty nor ugliness. When the mandate of Heaven approaches its end, one knows for oneself that one cannot maintain [the self]. To bind the time of death and the moment of birth—surely it accords with what is spoken.
Sitting steadily within the shrine, there is no need to flee. Cease this dull stupidity and listen as I analyze and explain.
"Eh! The West is your old path; there is no need for Amitābha to stretch out his hand.
Having finished this eulogy, the assembly was filled with profound sorrow and joy. They proceeded on their way until they reached the mountain mortuary office.
They halted at a shrine in the depths of a pine forest, where the five disciples then requested the Elder Hansokyan to perform the cremation. The Elder stood—
Standing atop the sedan chair, he held a torch in his hand and said: "All you people, listen!
This flickering flame is called 'Nameless. Whether you are startled while sitting within the coffin or not, you will only realize it is not a mistake when you look back.
If it is already clear, why bother asking others? He then paid his respects to the late Master Xingkong of Zixia Hall.
The Great Monk, Master Ben, Jueling, was originally a descendant of the Confucian lineage of Nanchang. Having taken refuge in the Chan school of this land, he has transcended worldly dust;
his nature is entirely empty, truly the seed of the Buddha’s family, possessing a harmonious air free from both joy and anger.
Possessing talent and learning, he dwelt with ease; alone he occupied a famous mountain, finding joy within it. Sixty-nine years were but a single dream.
Aha! Not following the flowing waters into Tiantai, he hastens by this flame-light back to the Pure Land.

Having finished his recitation, he raised a torch and set it ablaze. Ashes fell like rain, and from amidst the mass of flames, a monk appeared, rising into the air and crying out, "I owe you all a great debt of gratitude!
He spoke again, saying, "Li Maochun, your son is certainly not a government official;
he may only become a monk. Do not let him go astray by any means. If he does leave the household life, he should seek out Master Yian Xiatang at Mount Bingfeng."
He became my teacher and departed, riding upon the azure clouds. I have never forgotten the words of entrustment with which the Elder Yunqu Fen charged me when I was a youth;
thus, without realizing it, I reached the age of eight in the first year of the Yuan era. At that time, there was my maternal uncle Wang Anshi, who had a son ten years of age.
Zanshan then consulted with Anshi regarding the matter of inviting a teacher to instruct his son in the study of the *Yuan* and the classics.
There was no book he did not read. Gradually, when he reached the age of twelve, he could compose poems and fu upon merely picking up his brush.

When the Qingming festival arrived, Zanshan ordered a banquet to entertain the master and presented him with gold, silver, bolts of silk, and the traditional "fast-binding" offerings as a reward for his instruction.
The residence was not far away. The next day, the Zanshan (Court Gentleman) ordered his two sons to escort the Master back.
Upon returning to the gate of Jion-ji Temple, Wang Quan said, "Although you, my worthy brother, live nearby, you have never visited this temple.
Now that it is the season of Qingming, why do we not go in for some recreation? Would that not be appropriate? Xiuyuan replied, "How wonderful that would be! The two men went hand-in-hand inside.

He ascended the steps and entered the hall, walking all around the corridors. As he was about to enter the abbot’s quarters (fangzhang), he suddenly saw two men who said, "We are officials of the inner palace;
we pray that you, Master Xiaoshe, do not proceed. Xiu Yuan replied, "I am a secretary in the household of Minister Li Zanshan.
Who are these 'inner' people? I shall see them without hindrance. He then entered the abbot’s quarters and saw only a single bed therein. To its left...
One official sat on the left, and a monk sat on the right. Dozens of rows of acolytes stood lined up on both sides, each holding paper and brush.
Xiuyuan stepped forward and bowed, asking, "What are these many acolytes doing here? The Elder replied, "They are competing for merit."
Xiuyuan said, "I am but a young student; I do not understand what merit there is in this dispute.
The elder said, "This great man once traveled by sea and reached the Black Water Ocean, where suddenly a wild tempest arose. Only after making this vow did he manage to return home safely.
He then donated one thousand strings of cash to request a Daoist ordination certificate and have a monk tonsured, so that it might serve as a living practice."
The lyrics were fragmentary and incomplete, yet they formed a single song. Later, two lines were missing;
whoever could provide the continuation was to be tonsured as a monk. Xiu Yuan asked, "Where is this song? Please let me see it.
Because the official saw that Xiu Yuan’s appearance was refined and elegant, and his speech was graceful and spontaneous, he had the song brought out for him. Xiu Yuan took it and looked at it.
This is the "Manjianghong" (Full River Red) tune. The lyrics say:

"I have built a dwelling by the streams and mountains; upon inquiry, it is but a few thatched huts. Together we laugh and roam amidst the bright moon and clear breezes, as lush green shadows envelop the bamboo.
Sitting in stillness, I wash away the eyes of fame and profit; in weary sleep, my belly is always full of poetry and books. Let me be coarse..."
Wearing simple robes and eating plain rice, I pass my life; unencumbered, the clear days are long. Seeking out a chessboard, I play in the deep stillness of night;

tuning the strings of my lute, I calculate human affairs, which are like clouds turning and rain shifting. In the end, as Yuanming returned home, the three paths still held their autumn chrysanthemums.
I laugh at Bian He when he had not yet met the King of Chu—his jade remained a mere璞 (pó) in the mountains of Jing.
After Xiu Yuan finished reading it, he added two lines:
"Viewed with pure eyes, the three realms / Are all but a single thatched cottage.
When the official and the elder saw this, they were struck with amazement. They immediately invited Xiu Yuan and Wang Quan to sit down. The elder said:
"Two gentlemen, may I ask your names and where you reside? Ssu-yüan replied, "The elder brother is Prince An Wang-se;
the younger brother is Wang Chuan. As for this student, I am Li Ssu-yüan, son of the Court Gentleman Li. The Elder said, "I know, I know.
Over ten years ago, on the day the Elder of Kuo-ch'ing Temple passed away, he spoke with your honorable father, saying that the young master—"

"You may leave the household life. Since you have continued these verses today, it is only logical that you should shave your head and become a monk. Xiu Yuan said, "My father has begotten me as his only son, a student;
how could there be any reason for me to leave the household life? The Elder said, "I, this poor monk, shall build a dwelling for you myself."
"Seeing that my honored father has sent word to invite you, how could I dare to act so hastily today? If the two young masters do not reject me, you may stay for one night at our humble temple.
Xuanyuan replied, "I am returning the Master from whom I received my studies; the route passes through this eminent monastery.
I have merely taken half a day’s leave. My father does not know of this; how would I dare to act on my own authority? The Elder saw him out of the mountain gate and returned to the abbot’s quarters.

He said to the official, "This boy is no ordinary man; his future cannot be measured. If you, Excellency, would grant one thousand *guan* so that he may be tonsured, it would serve both to enhance your reputation as a great man and to bring glory to this humble monk. I do not know whether this boy will be willing to leave the household life.
Now, let us speak of the brothers Xiuyuan and his sibling; they returned to their residence to pay their respects to their parents. Zanshan said:
"You two, get out! Why have you returned so late? Xiu-yuan replied, "We were most grateful for the wine you, Master, provided us.
On our way back, we passed through Jiyuan Temple and went inside to visit. We happened upon a group of novice monks in the abbot’s quarters competing for merit."

The boy immediately composed two lines of verse. Because of this delay, the elder of that temple said he would come in person the following day to inform his father. The Zanshan said, "My son knows only one thing, but not the second.
Within Mount Tiantai, there are over three hundred temples. Previously, the elder of Guoqing Temple, the Chan master Xingkong..."
"Master, both the Master and the Venerable Han-yan have already passed away. Recently, the Elder of Jiyuan Temple has been honored;
how could one possibly slight him? Wang Quan said, "Father, why worry?
Your child also knows that my younger brother’s two lines of verse have just now startled that elder. If he comes tomorrow, your child will have a response ready."
Zanshan smiled and desisted. The following morning, it was suddenly reported that the Elder of Jiyuan Temple had arrived. Zanshan went out to welcome him.
After the formal greetings were concluded, the Elder said, "Yesterday, when your son visited our temple, he happened upon some novice monks competing for merit.
He moved me by completing a verse for them; therefore, I have come specifically to request that your noble son enter the monastic order. No sooner had he finished speaking than—
"What is your honorable intention? Zanshan replied, "I am deeply grateful for your superior virtue; my appreciation is beyond measure.

However, as for this one son of yours, it is difficult for me to comply with your command. The Elder said, "There is a proverb that says: 'If one son leaves the household life, nine generations of his clan ascend to heaven.
Furthermore, why do you suddenly forget the words of the Elder Xingkong from more than ten years ago?"

In the midst of their conversation, Xu Yuan suddenly emerged from behind the screen. After he had stepped forward and completed his salutation, he said, "I am deeply grateful for the Elder’s great kindness;
however, as a student, I have three matters that make it difficult for me to leave the household life. The Elder asked, "What are they? Xu Yuan replied:
"The student has not yet reached the age of twenty (the *guan* ceremony). He is unacquainted with formal affairs, and his parents are at home without anyone to provide for them.
Having examined the monastic community of Tiantai, I find no one fit to be my teacher. For these three reasons, it is difficult for me to accept your command.
The Elder said, "I am already sixty years old; why should I not be able to be your teacher? Xiu-yuan replied, "The student has a saying:"
He spoke, addressing the Elder: "Elder, you are young; why such wild behavior? Xiu-yuan stepped forward and said, "Venerable sir, what is your age?

The Elder replied, "I am sixty-two years old. Xiu-yuan said, "Since you are sixty-two years old, I do not know where that single point of spiritual light has been all this time. The Elder was abashed and had no reply.
After a long silence, Xiu Yuan said, "If you have not yet attained awakening through this single phrase, how can you be my teacher?
The Elder was struck with fear and found himself with no place to stand. He praised Sandai’s excellent meal, but he firmly declined to remain and returned to his temple.
He felt uneasy in his heart and lay down for three consecutive days. Upon rising, it was suddenly announced that Daojing, the Elder of Guanyin Temple, had come to visit him. They met.
Once they were seated and the tea was finished, [Dōgen] said, "I have heard that you, elder brother, have been unwell in body; I have come specifically to pay my respects.

I do not know what caused you to fall ill. Dōkyō, the Elder, replied, "I am deeply grateful for your kind intentions. It is difficult to explain in a single word; let me describe it to you in detail."
Daojing said, "If it is like this, what difficulty could there be? Daoqing said, "Worthy brother, do not underestimate him.
This youth’s talent and learning are truly outstanding. While they were speaking, a report arrived that Li Zanshan and his son had both come to visit. The Elder said:
"Please enter. After the ceremony was concluded, tea was served. Zanshan said, "Young sir, yesterday the mad Pei committed an offense against his superior;
you, Master, released your anger out of compassion. Daoqing said, "I am deeply humbled, I am deeply humbled. Daoning said, "The young gentleman here is he. Daoqing said, "Indeed.
Daoning said, "The young gentleman’s appearance is most distinguished. Yuan said, "My name is Xiuyuan. Daoning said, "What is your courtesy name?"
Xiu Yuan’s original destiny was difficult to cultivate. Xiu Yuan said with indignation, "My name is Daojing. 'Jing' (purity) gives rise to the Ultimate Bliss;
the Way requires precepts. The two superiors rose in reverence. Daoqing waited until the meal was finished before the Zanshan returned.
Every day Xiu Yuan would compose poetry in the academy, unaware that his years had already reached twenty-eight. Who could have foreseen that his wife...
The Wang family fell ill and was unable to rise; she passed away at the age of fifty-one.

By the time her mother’s period of mourning had concluded, she had also completed the mourning period for her father. Her maternal uncle, Wang Anshi, repeatedly proposed marriage to Yuan, yet Yuan remained unconcerned.
At that time, he visited various monasteries, seeking only the two elders, Master Yin of Biefeng and Yuan Xiatang, but he knew nothing of their whereabouts.
After half a year had passed, he finally received news: Master Yin of Biefeng was serving as abbot at Jingshan Temple in Lin’an;
Yuan Xiatang had previously served as abbot at Tiger Hill in Suzhou and was now at Lingyin Temple. He first informed his maternal uncle, Wang An.

Shi said, "This matter is not necessarily entirely virtuous, nor is it necessarily true. However, among all the many properties of your family, who else besides you and your younger brothers would be capable of managing them?
Yuan replied, "I am fortunate to have a worthy elder brother who manages the household affairs so well."
"I expect there will be no hindrance. We shall certainly set out on the auspicious day of the thirteenth of the second month.
An-se said, "If we are to depart so urgently, it is necessary to have our clothing properly prepared. I am extremely old; therefore, let Wang Quan go with you.
Yuan said, "There is no one else at home. Why must my worthy elder brother go? A mere one or two attendants would suffice. The auspicious day had already arrived.
Huiyuan took several bundles of cash and, having paid his respects and taken leave of his maternal uncle, set out. Anshi instructed him repeatedly, and Huiyuan received each word with full attention.
Traveling by stages, he crossed the Qiantang River, disembarked, and entered the city, proceeding directly to a guesthouse at Xinguo Bridge where he rested.
The following morning, accompanied by Wang Quan and carrying his attendants, he wandered about the city for sightseeing. By evening, he returned and said to his host:
The man said, "I have long admired the magnificent sights of Lin’an. I, a humble person, have come specifically for some leisurely sightseeing.
The host replied, "In this city, there are nothing but government offices and yamen. What good is there in the streets and shops?

If you wish for diversion, why not go to the various temples on the two mountains to the southwest? The scenic beauty of West Lake is rarely found anywhere in the world. Yuan said, "There is one spirit..."
"Where, then, is Lingyin Monastery? The host replied, "This monastery is located directly opposite Feilai Peak on the western hills.
Yuan asked, "By what path can one reach it? The host said, "Upon exiting the Qiantang Gate, you will find West Lake.
Pass beneath Baoshu Pagoda and follow the northern shore of the lake until you reach the tomb of Marshal Yue Wumu; entering west from there is Lingyin Monastery. Before it..."
Stone Buddha Grotto, Cold Spring Pavilion, and Howling Ape Grotto—there are endless beautiful sights; the waters are clear and the mountains are exquisite.
Yuan asked, "How many monks are there in this monastery? The host replied, "There are approximately three to five hundred.
Last year, the presiding elder passed away and went to Mount Huqiu in Gusu. We have invited a monk named Yuan Xiatang; this monk is skilled..."
He knew of past and future events. Yuan said, "I shall go to see him early tomorrow morning.
Yuan then disguised himself as a scholar and, accompanied by an attendant, traveled along the road out through the Qiantang Gate. It was the third month; the weather was bright and pleasant.
Yuan looked back at his attendant and said, "I have heard descriptions of the scenery of Hangzhou’s West Lake; it truly does not disappoint. They entered Zhaokong Temple.
Beholding the image of Great Compassion, the verse says:
When one hand moves, a thousand hands move; When one eye looks, a thousand eyes look.
Since you are already named Avalokiteśvara, Why must you display so many various gestures?
Having finished his inscription, he proceeded to the Great Buddha Temple. Seeing the half-body of the Great Buddha, he composed this verse:
"Leaning his back against the cold crags, His face like the full moon— All the people of the great earth See but a single half.
Having finished his inscription, he traveled on to Feilai Peak and sat at Cold Spring Pavilion. Beside the Yuan-yang Pavilion, there was a tablet of a Tang-era worthy.
The poem by Bai Juyi says:
"The north wind is piercing and the snow falls vast; Yet it does not compare to the chill of a single stream of clear water.
In the midsummer heat, no rain falls from the sky; I ask you, sir, to lean here against this balustrade."
Xiuyuan gazed at the beautiful scenery with unending admiration. Seeing many monks following the elder straight into the temple, he was the only one left behind.
Xiuyuan hurried forward to pay his respects, asking, "From where did this elder just come?
The monk replied, "He is the newly appointed abbot of this monastery, Elder Yuan Xiatang. Because of Mount Jingci Temple..."
Yin was returning to Xibing when he heard that Yuan had gone down to extinguish the fire; only then did he return. Yuan said, "I, a student, wish to see the Elder.
I venture to trouble you for an introduction. The Abbot went forward to inform the Elder, who then invited him to enter. Yuan proceeded to have an audience.
After the formalities were completed, the Elder asked, "Where has the scholar come from? Yuan replied, "Your disciple has come specifically from Mount Tiantai. He then related his lineage.

He was a descendant of the late Imperial Prince Li and the son of the Court Gentleman for Propriety. His childhood name was Xiuyuan. Having the misfortune of losing both his parents, he resolved to leave the household life.
Recently, hearing that my master had traveled with his staff, he came specifically to pay his respects and seek refuge, entreating me to cast a pure eye upon him.

The Elder said, "If you do not yet know that leaving the household life is easy while sitting in meditation is difficult, consider that there are more than three hundred monasteries on Mount Tiantai."
"Why do you abandon what is near to pursue what is far? Yuan replied, "In my youth, I received the final instructions of the Elder of Guoqing Temple;
therefore, I have come specifically to pay my respects. The Elder asked, "Who will attend to me after you are gone? Yuan replied, "I shall take a humble servant from my home to serve as my disciple."
The Elder said, "Each family has its own means, great or small; you should send them back at once.

Yuan then took out some of the banknotes he was carrying and handed them over to the Elder, intending for them to serve as expenses for providing vegetarian feasts, requesting ordination certificates, and the general maintenance of the monastery.

He entrusted the remainder to his servants as travel funds for the journey home. The servants said, "We have followed and served you, Master, all the way to this place, hoping against hope to return home in fine robes.
We never expected that you would instead leave the household life here at this temple. Yuan said, "It was only right that you should have returned far away.
Convey my words to my maternal uncle: I have left the household life at Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou. The two servants shed tears profusely.
Unable to bear the parting, he spoke briefly while the Elder was in the abbot’s quarters.

He ordered an attendant to burn incense and light candles, then sat upright in his meditation chair and entered *samādhi* for half an hour. He then said, "Excellent, excellent! This very karmic affinity lies here indeed.

Thereupon, he selected an auspicious day, prepared a vegetarian feast, and requested a *du-chie* (ordination certificate). When the feast concluded, the bells and drums were struck to assemble the congregation at the Dharma hall.
In the hall, the Elder told Lingyuan to kneel beneath the Dharma seat and said, "Leaving the household life is easy; returning to secular life is difficult. Do you understand this?

Having disembarked, Ji Gong thought to himself, "If I go to another temple, they will not treat me with the same respect.
I am originally from Lingyin; I shall go straight there to see if this pack of shaven-headed brats will accept me.
He then crossed Ciyun Ridge and went directly to Lingyin Temple. Upon reaching Feilai Peak, he saw a Librarian (Zangzhu), who said, "Ji Gong!"
"You have been away from Tiantai for a long time. The abbot of the temple has changed;
the elder Chang is now in charge, popularly known as 'Tanbantou' (The Head of the Wooden Blocks). Ji Gong said, "In that case, it will be difficult to join their ranks.
He went straight to the temple and arrived at the mountain gate, where he saw a senior monk (shouzuo) who said, "Ji Gong, you have come. The current elder is not like your teacher."
Father, Master Ji said, "If I can secure some benefit, I will not fear you bullying me.
The Head Seat said, "I shall accompany you to see the Elder. The two arrived at the Abbot’s quarters and saw the Elder; Master Ji prostrated himself.
The Head Seat stepped forward and said, "This monk is the disciple of the former abbot, Venerable Yuan; his name is Daoji. Because he has returned—"
When Tiantai had been away for over a year, he finally returned. The Elder said, "Could this not be that Jie who can drink wine?

Jie Gong replied, "I, your disciple, have been traveling for a year; I have completely abstained from both wine and meat. The Elder said, "If that is so, you may register your name here and surrender your ordination certificate.
Jie Gong remained in the Yun-tang hall to practice *zazen*, and during his leisure time, he recited [sutras] in the main hall.
After more than two months had passed, he did not emerge from the mountain gate again. It was then the end of winter, and a great snow fell.
Master Ji felt his body grow cold, so he went to the Xiangji kitchen and sat down by the fire, baring a pair of shapely legs.
The fire-attendant said, "Your master has many robes and bowls for you, yet people have taken them away. In such heavy snow as this, [how can you remain] with only a pair of shapely..."
"The legs are not cold," [the laborers] said. Jigong replied, "The cold is what I must endure; being frozen does not matter.
It is only the suffering of not drinking wine for over a year that troubles me. When the laborers saw how Jigong spoke with such heartfelt distress, they said, "Jigong!"
"We have some wine here; please drink it. [The host] feared that the Elder would find out. Ji Gong said, "Brother, it is rare to meet such a kind heart.
I shall hide under the stove while I drink; one person will screen me from view while the other pours the wine.
After Ji Gong had drunk, he walked out from the kitchen. Indeed, this wine was harmless as long as it was not consumed.
Having eaten, he became bold and disregarded the Elder’s words; he went straight out before the mountain gate and happened upon Zhang Gong, who resided beneath the signboard at Flying Peak.
Zhang Gong said, "Ji Gong, it has been a long time since we last saw you. Ji Gong replied, "Grandfather, there is no need to speak of it.
I have come from Taizhou and have been at this temple for over a year," to which the Elder detained him.
He was bound so tightly that he did not dare leave the temple gates. Today, by chance, he went down to the kitchen, where the cook invited him to drink a bottle of wine.
Finding it quite flavorful, he specifically came out to seek a host. Zhang Gong said, "How about coming to my house for three cups?
Ji Gong replied, "That would be excellent. Following Zhang Gong, he went straight to Feilai Peak. Zhang...
The old woman was standing at the gate when she saw Laozi leading Ji Gong toward her. Overjoyed, she exclaimed, "I have not seen you for a long time, Master!
They all went inside. The old woman served two bowls of tofu and brewed a pot of wine. The two men sat opposite each other while her son poured the wine.
Ji Gong said, "Father, it is rare indeed that you, Mother, and this entire family possess such kind hearts. The old woman replied, "It is so."
"Dao, the Master has passed away in another way; there is only this wine here. You just go ahead and drink.
One bowl for you, one bowl for me; let us each drink fifteen or sixteen bowls. When they felt intoxicated, Ji Gong rose and shouted, "Nao! (Enough!)
The old woman said, "It is already this late. Your Elder saw that you were not permitted to drink wine; you must go back now.
If you come back again, I will not know how to show you respect—not even for me. Jigong said, "Old woman, what you say is right.
I shall simply stay here with your son for one night. The next morning, Jigong saw that the weather was clear and bright.

For a long time he had not entered the city; looking toward his friends, he thought, "Today I shall make a visit. Having eaten breakfast at Zhang Gong’s house, he went straight to Yue Feng (the Tomb of Yue Fei).
Just as he was passing through, he ran right into two parties. As Ji Gong stood still to watch, it turned out to be Imperial Protector Wang.
Seeing Ji Gong, the Imperial Protector hurriedly descended from his sedan chair and said, "Why have we not seen each other for so long?"
Jigong recounted the preceding events in detail. The Grand Marshal said, "I am going to Tiantzhu today;
I cannot return to your residence with you. You may come to the residence once tomorrow morning. Jigong replied, "Much obliged, much obliged.
Once the Grand Marshal had mounted his palanquin and departed, Jigong entered the Qiantang Gate by himself and went straight to the riverbank at Tanqiao.
Ji Gong arrived at the Shen Family Inn. At that time, the innkeeper was not present. Seeing Ji Gong, the manager hurriedly said, "Please, come inside and sit.
My master has been thinking of you constantly; let my son come out to attend to you. After the tea service was completed, the son approached.
Seeing that the Superintendent had not returned, Ji Gong intended to go back to the temple. Suddenly, snowflakes began to fall in swirling patterns. Looking up, Ji Gong composed a poem, saying:
"From the distant bay, a chilling mass of clouds arises; In the vast sky, shattered jade tinkles and falls. Pear blossoms fill my eyes, drifting upon the waves."
Lan. The water is deep; the back of the giant tortoise is cold. The old monk of Fangzhang shivers. Travelers at the ferry crossing sigh.

This realm of Jinsan has transformed into a silver mountain. Jade towers, crystal palaces, and bowls of water-ice—though Wang Wei excels at painting, even he would find it difficult to capture them with his brush.
The above is in the tune "Linjiangshan."
Having finished writing the title, he pondered that Inspector Shen must be at the Lacquerware Bridge, at the residence of Wang Xingxian and his family.
Early the next morning, without taking leave of his son, he went straight toward the Lacquerware Bridge. Upon arriving at the house, he asked the daughter-in-law, "Is Inspector Shen at your home?
The daughter-in-law replied, "He has just now gone out to bathe. Ji Gong said, "In that case, I—"
He waited for her. Then he went upstairs to see that the courtesan was fast asleep.
Ji Gong gently pulled back the covers, stepped onto the bed, took a small shoe, and placed it upon her private parts. He then descended the stairs, where he happened to run into Inspector Shen.
The Inspector said, "I have not seen you for a long time; why are you here? Ji Gong replied, "Yesterday I came specifically..."
I came seeking you, but you were not at home. I presumed you would surely be here; I rose early and came specifically for this purpose.
Yet you have gone to bathe, so I missed your welcome. For now, let us go upstairs to eat breakfast. When the two of them went upstairs together, the courtesan Wang was just waking up.
Seeing these shoes, she felt uneasy in her heart and asked, "Who has come upstairs? The maid replied: [The text provided ends here.]
Jigong said, "Venerable Director, what kind of principle is this for one who has left the household life? Jigong replied, "Forbearance, forbearance!
It is not that I am being impolite; there is a certain karmic connection. The Director said, "I wish to hear it. Jigong then recited a lyric:
The butterfly grows weary of clinging to the flower branches; having fallen asleep, the spring dream is difficult to awaken from. The silken robe is cast off and no longer follows the body;

the three souls wander through the Langyuan Gardens, while the seven spirits roam around Mount Penglai. Thus, one takes the silken shoes to block the mouth of the cave, for one must know that after awakening, resentment will arise.
This is not because of a lack of spiritual salvation or feigned human sentiment; it is to sever the path of birth and death and cut it off forever.
The Gate of Right and Wrong. (Right: A *Línjiāngxiān* [Song of the River Goddess]).
The Inspector laughed heartily and said, "An excellent composition. He had a serving girl bring three bowls of *diǎnduò* wine.
Ji Gong drank one bowl and remarked, "It is not effective. The head courtesan said, "I will not drink; you drink them all. Ji Gong drank again.
"A bowl. Your daughter brought the morning meal; the two of them ate it. Ji Gong said, "Thank you, thank you.
Lord Wang Taewei on Wansong Ridge expects me to come today. Let us go see him for a moment.
The Superintendent said, "When we return, stop by my house first. Ji Gong went straight to Qinghefang. Upon reaching Zongyang Palace, he proceeded further.
Opposite the wine cellar, he saw a tofu shop with a good business. He pushed his way in and rushed inside.
Seeing the snow beginning to fall, Ji Gong thought, "I shall go buy some bowls of it to eat. Once Ji Gong was seated, the innkeeper asked, "Monk, how much will you have?
Ji Gong replied, "Just a bit at random. The innkeeper then set out four dishes of vegetables and one plate of tofu.
One jar of wine. One bowl. Ji Gong drank one jar and found the wine to be flavorful.
He took another jar and drank it; then he wanted yet another. The innkeeper said, "Monk, my wine is strong; you can only drink two jars.
Ji Gong replied, "What does that matter to you? Just keep pouring! He drank two more jars. Ji Gong—
He had not a single coin on his person; his gaze fell only upon the lay donor before the gate.
It happened to be snowing, and passersby were few. When the tavern keeper came to collect the money, Jigong said, "I did not bring any with me.
Let me have credit. The tavern keeper replied, "This monk is truly unreasonable. Who do you think you are? Jigong said, "I am—"
The monk from Lingyin Temple told the innkeeper to send someone along with him, and the innkeeper replied, "I do not have that much time;
I shall take off this tattered cassock of mine and give it to you. Ji Gong said, "I am calling for vegetable dumplings;
they must be wrapped in these very skins. How can you take them off? As the two men struggled at the door, across the street was the Shengyang Palace.
From atop the wine house, the people saw the monk being led by the innkeeper; he looked like Ji Gong.

He immediately ordered his attendant to go and call the two men up. When the innkeeper and Ji Gong reached the floor of the building opposite, Ji Gong observed that they were indeed the brothers of Inspector Shen—Shen Wuguan and [his brother]. Ji Gong said, "You are enjoying yourself here, while I have been..."
He clung to him, demanding payment for the wine. Shen Wuguan said, "I saw you from afar; that is why I have come specifically to invite you.
Ji Gong replied, "It is a bit late now; this piece of yellow skin has been stripped off. Everyone laughed heartily.
Shen Wuguan instructed the wine steward to go back and pay Ji Gong’s bill. Once the steward had left, Ji Gong—
He said, "Nonsense! Brother, untie this knot. Shen Wuguan said, "In such heavy snow, let us sit together with the Head of the Bureau for a while.
The three of them began drinking from the beginning again. Ji Gong was already tipsy; after drinking just a few cups, he felt somewhat intoxicated.
Wuguan said, "You were just now begging for such a favor; why not compose a poem as a toast? Ji Gong then—
He composed four lines of verse, saying:
"Habituated to feasting on alms, I seek a patron; Yet the few coins about me do not amount to a single cent.
Who would have known that I have run into a true business associate? Were it not for this donor, how could I escape?"
Regarding the five senses and the way of humanity, how many bowls will you eat? Ji Gong then recited another four lines:
"In my life I have only loved drinking yellow wine; For several days I had no money to buy some to taste.
Now that I am fortunate to meet you, do not refuse me; I beg for a few more bowls to moisten my parched gut."
The warden laughed heartily and ordered the wine steward to focus solely on pouring the ale. Ji Gong drank more than ten bowls and then composed another four-line verse:
"In days of yore, I heard of Li Zhe Xian, Who drank a pint of wine and penned a hundred poems."
"I am moved by your generous gift, free from any stinginess; how could this poor monk ever let saliva flow at the sight?
Inspector Li laughed heartily. The attendants again poured wine for Ji Gong to drink. Ji Gong was greatly pleased and composed another four-line verse:
Since I arrived, my capacity for wine has known no bounds; Only this pit of poverty can never be filled.
If you wish to lie by the side of the vat like Bi Zhuo, I bid you seek another thirty bowls.
The Five Officials saw that Ji Gong was drunk and called the on-call attendant to give orders. They told three singers to perform.
Before long, three singers arrived; one sat beside Wuguān, and another sat beside Inspector Li.
Wuguān said, "Jigong, seeing that you are so composed and cool, I have specially invited this lady to accompany you.
Jigong replied, "Very well," and composed a poem, saying:
Every day he greedily drinks wine and stays with courtesans; What an extraordinary, licentious monk!
His cassock is often stained with rouge, And the scent of fragrant powder is frequently heard from his vestments.
The Innkeeper said, "There is no one here. Master Ji, you may sleep with my lady. Just then, the innkeeper came up.
As she approached, he would not let her pass. Master Ji recited a quatrain:
The jade blossoms in the storehouse vie in their brilliant colors; Among them, one flower is most worthy of pity.
Though it possesses ten thousand kinds of elegant grace, Only its Zen-mind remains as firm as iron.
Wu Guan said with delight, "Truly a fine composition. Ji Gong then recited another quatrain:
"In the past, my parents assumed this manner, To give birth to this stinking skin-sack of mine.
My heart is not like my parents' heart; My heart loves nothing except wine."
Having finished his verses, he drank several more bowls of wine. As evening gradually fell, Wuguan said, "Jigong, it is late; you will not be able to return to the temple.
Wuguan ordered the on-duty attendant to support Jigong down from the tower, and after bidding farewell to Director Li, the two went straight to the home of Liu Hangxiu on New Street.
The matriarch received them with great joy and said, "Wuguan, today..."
The Five Officials asked, "How did you bring this drunken monk, Master Feng, with you?

The old woman said, "He was late and could not return to his temple, so he came along to borrow a place to rest. The old woman replied, "That is no matter," and immediately called her two daughters to meet him and ordered wine to be prepared.
The Five Officials said, "We are already drunk. The Five Officials then ordered their eldest daughter to go to sleep with Ji Gong. The Five...
The official slept with the second sister. The eldest sister pushed Ji Gong into the room; he sat upon the bed and locked the door.
She began to undress Ji Gong, but he cried out, "Alas! What a transgression! I have been so tightly bound that my wine has sobered me.
He rose, opened the door, and was about to flee, fearing he might be caught by the night watchmen. Just then, he saw Spring...
On the edge of the platform was a large firebox that was somewhat warm; he crawled inside and lay down on his side to sleep.
His elder sister also went off to sleep by herself. Hearing the bells of Chao Tian Men toll, Ji Gong hurriedly scrambled up, pushed open the window, and looked out;
the eastern sky had already begun to brighten. He then composed a quatrain:
Borrowing for a night the sleep of husband and wife, The mind of meditation and lustful desire are not linked.
Last night I yielded to your noble intent, Giving the old woman five strings of cash.
Having finished the verse, he saw a jug of leftover wine from the previous night upon the table. He drank it all and then composed another poem:
Verse: From of old, all matters have been unrelated; I alone truly crave this fragrant wine.
If I did not have three bowls of wine at dawn, How could I withstand the biting north wind outside my gate?
After Ji Gong finished writing, he opened the main gate and departed down a path.
Hearing the sound of the door, the old woman hurriedly rose to look; she saw only a sheet of paper on the stand while Dajie was fast asleep.
When she questioned her, Dajie said, "Last night it was like this and like that. The old woman remarked, "Truly a young man! Shortly thereafter, Wuguan arose.
Ji Gong was asked by the pious old woman, "He left early. On the table lay a strip of paper with writing upon it.
As soon as Wuguan saw it, he said, "This does not belie the status of one who has left the household life. Meanwhile, Ji Gong stepped through the ice and emerged from Qingbo Gate.
Thinking to himself, "Now my body is cold and my stomach is hungry; I shall go to Wansong Ridge to find a patron and beg for some breakfast."
Having finished his meal, he went straight to the front of Minister Chen’s residence. He saw a gatekeeper sweeping the ground. Master Ji said, "Please announce my arrival for me.
The gatekeeper then set aside his broom and went inside to report. Minister Chen hurriedly rose and went directly to the main hall.
Master Ji stepped forward to pay his respects. The Minister asked, "Why have we not seen each other for so long? Master Ji replied, "I have returned."
I returned to the temple for the year-end festival and was bound tightly by the elders. A few days ago, I obtained three bowls of wine from a fire-worker and drank it, which stirred my thoughts.
For several days, I have been amusing myself idly with Shen Wuguan in the city. Yesterday, I went to Xinjie and stayed at Liu Hangxiu’s house;
I rose early and fled, coming specifically to the Prefectural Office. The Grand Marshal laughed heartily and took [me in].
The soup arrived. Ji Gong said, "I do not wish to eat the soup. The Grand Marshal said, "I understand that you only wish to drink wine.
He ordered the official on duty to prepare delicacies, wine, and fruit. Ji Gong drank fifteen or sixteen bowls. The Grand Marshal asked, "Is your body cold?
Ji Gong replied, "Let this stubborn skin-sack freeze as it will. The Grand Marshal said, "You..."
On his body he wore a single tattered *zhiduo* robe; on his feet were a pair of worn-out monk’s sandals. Bare and naked, his two legs were exposed.

"I shall now give you a bolt of patterned silk and a roll of official silk to make yourself a garment," [the donor said], "and one *liang* of silver for the tailor's fee. Ji Gong replied, "I have no way to repay you. Next winter..."
"There is a great calamity at hand. Bring me paper and brush. Fetch an incense box. Let all bystanders withdraw for a moment.

Ji Gong then wrote some characters and placed them inside the incense box. He sealed it according to the prescribed ritual and gave it to the Grand Marshal, instructing him to place it before the Buddha hall.
"When a disaster strikes next year," he said, "you may open it and look within. Subsequently, the Grand Marshal suddenly fell ill with a carbuncle on his back.
It was as large as a tea bowl and the pain was unbearable. Despite a hundred kinds of medical treatments, it would not heal.
Suddenly, he remembered the incense box left behind by Ji Gong. He hurriedly took it out to look; inside the box was written a prescription for "Taiwei" (Grand Marshal).
He then prepared the medicine according to the instructions and immediately obtained a cure. This is a later story. Let us now speak of how Ji Gong obtained the silk on that day.

Having finished paying his respects to the Grand Commandant with the official silk and silver, he had only just descended the ridge when he saw a group of beggars frozen to the ground. Ji Gong said, "How miserable! I have some things for you.

Reaching into his sleeve, he pulled out the brocade, the official silk, and the silver, giving them all to the crowd. Continuing on his way back to Lingyin Temple, he saw the Head Seat and said, "You..."
"Where have you been? Jigong replied, "For several days now I have been drinking wine at Shengyang Tower and staying with courtesans in Xinjie Village.
The Head Seat said, "Very well; you go on drinking wine and sleeping with courtesans.
Jigong said, "I go openly; is that not better than going in the dark as you do? The Head Seat said, "The Elder asked me yesterday, and I—"
It was said that you had been visiting the sixteen provincial officials. It turns out you have been acting so recklessly! He hurriedly dragged him into the abbot’s quarters to see the Elder.
The Elder stated that Ji Gong had gone out on his own to drink wine and stay with prostitutes. The Elder was furious and ordered an attendant to give him twenty blows.
As the attendant dragged him down and lifted up his *zhizhi* robe, he discovered that Ji Gong was not wearing any trousers; he simply turned around.
He exposed the object before them, and the assembly of monks laughed heartily. The Elder said, "This fellow is so impudent.
The Head Seat said, "The late Master was protective of him; he has grown accustomed to such behavior.
The Elder said, "There is no need to strike this madman; let him go for now. Ji Gong laughed loudly and, leaving the abbot’s quarters, said, "You all..."
"Drag me before the Elder; he will not beat me. You fine fellow! I shall wrestle with you three times! The monks said, "We have no use for you, you madman.
Ji Gong replied, "You bandits! Yet you are afraid of me. From then on, he became even more deranged.
All the monks came together to consult with the Elder as to how they might drive him out. The Elder—
He said, "This man is the disciple of our former master. How can we drive him away? The Prior said, "I have a plan that will naturally leave him with no place to settle.

The assembly asked, "What is it? The Prior said, "Previously, there was a solicitor for salt and vegetables in the monastery who collected them daily for the common use of the community. This office is the most difficult; he must go out to solicit."
"It cannot be done; he would be ashamed to turn back. We should now buy a jar of wine and prepare a feast to make him thoroughly drunk.
If he consents, it will not take more than a month or so. The monks said, "A brilliant plan! We only fear he may not agree."
The Chief Administrator said, "He simply wants to drink wine. That day, he prepared a vegetarian feast and set out wine, inviting Ji Gong to drink.
When Ji Gong arrived at the abbot’s quarters and was seated, he asked, "Elder, why did you summon me?
The Elder replied, "The monks have purchased wine here and invited you. Ji Gong said, "That is quite strange. Tell me, for what reason did you invite me? The Elder...

He said, "When I first took up residence as abbot, I was unaware of these prior matters. Previously, there was someone who served as the solicitor for salt and vegetables, but now there has been no one at all.
I wish to appoint a solicitor now and require you to draft the introductory petition; for this reason, I invite you."
Jigong said, "Since you wish to write the petition, simply drink wine; only when one is drunk does one possess true literary talent. The Elder said, "You do nothing but eat.
At that moment, the attendant placed a large bowl before Jigong, who consumed thirty-odd bowls in a single sitting.
He then paused for a while. The attendant subsequently set forth the Four Treasures of the Writing Studio upon the table.
He ground the ink thickly. Jigong rose, brushed his paper, and composed the text without adding a single stroke, saying:
"Prostrate: Throughout the day, time passes swiftly; food and clothing are difficult to obtain. Within the gates of the Empty Gate (the monastic order), all rely upon the *dānapati* (donors);
within the temples, everything depends entirely upon the patrons. Were there no patrons, the buildings would collapse to the east and west; were there no *dānapati*..."
Therefore, the Master endures hunger and cold; his robes are not of brocade or silk, yet he must have cotton cloth to cover his body;
his food is not of delicacies, yet he must rely on sour pickles and thin gruel. Although his expenses are not luxurious, it is difficult for many people to sustain him.
I venture to present this brief memorial to knock at your lofty gates. I do not come to beg for the gift of robes or grain, but rather—
I merely prepare some salted vegetables; the potter labors diligently at his kiln and the gardener toils wearily in his orchard.
I am ashamed to beg of them with a foolish face, relying entirely upon their kind assistance. Do not take offense that this poor monk speaks so much every morning;
it is because our wretched temple relies on them for its daily sustenance. Without them, how could there be even a bowl of coarse rice gruel?
Sent into the hungry bowels: half a plate of yellow, sour pickled vegetables. Only with you can one satisfy a starving mouth. You, O Monk, are a vessel of *prajñā*;

you, a high official, universally give rise to a heart of joy. Daily, eight strings of cash are offered as resources to provide for the permanent residence of the Sangha, increasing its wealth and honor.
Morning by morning, we are honored by the Three Jewels and the worthy sages; we pray that the patron may enjoy eternal peace and security. Respectfully.
Jigong wrote the date at the bottom of the scroll.
Having finished, the Elder and the assembly of monks all shouted in approval, ordering the novice to fetch wine.
Jigong drank another ten or more bowls. The Elder said, "One guest should not trouble two hosts; I further trouble you to compose one more."
The Master of Fundraising asked, "Jigong, you say you are a 'Wind-Son' (a madman); how could you possibly succeed at this?
The Prior replied, "Jigong associates with high-ranking officials from the sixteen ministries and eighteen wealthy patrons.
Do not speak of eight strings of cash a day; even eighty strings, he can raise them. The Elder said, "I see, so that is how it is. Jigong said, "It is among those I know personally."
"Stop this fondness for soliciting wine and food; why do you go on begging for money?
The Elder said, "You have been begging recklessly for six months or three months; I shall now have someone else take over your duties. At that moment, Ji Gong was already intoxicated.
"I have already consumed your wine; how can you deny it? The Elder was greatly pleased and immediately provided incense, flowers, and lamps.

He invited Ji Gong to sit and received three prostrations from the Elder. Having prepared offerings of vegetarian food and fruit, he took his leave of the Elder and departed from the abbot’s quarters.
To himself he thought: "I have been outmaneuvered; staying here will serve no purpose."
"It is not as good as issuing a *dùcí* (ordination certificate) all at once and going elsewhere. [He] turned back toward the abbot’s quarters.
The Elder asked why he had returned again. Jigong said, 'I was thinking of acting as this fundraiser so that I would never have to go begging for alms elsewhere;
however, since I have no *dùcí* on my person, people simply take me for a wild monk. That is why I have come back to fetch one.'"
The Elder said, "What you say is correct. He immediately ordered the monastery supervisor to fetch the ordination certificate and hand it over to Ji Gong, who took it and departed on his own.
Now, let us speak of Ji Gong as he left the mountain gate and went straight to sit by the Bailuo Bridge. He thought to himself, "This pack of shaven-headed brutes has formed a circle to seize me;
it is clearly a trap to lure me out. The Elder Dehui of Jingci Temple has always been on friendly terms with me."
"It is fitting. If I go to seek him, he will surely grant me his presence. He proceeded directly toward Jingci Temple.
Upon entering, he paid his respects to the Elder. The Elder asked, "Where have you come from, Ji Gong? Ji Gong replied, "It cannot be told.
Your disciple was conscripted by the assembly to serve as the solicitor for salt and vegetables. At first, I was unwilling, but later they intoxicated me with wine, and in a moment, I complied."
[Zhao] Cheng: "Now I wish to know that you are constrained by me as I go out the door; therefore, I have come specifically to seek refuge with you, hoping you will keep me as your beloved.
The Elder said: "You belong to Lingyin Temple; you have your own kin and followers there. Why have you come out empty-handed? Jigong said: "I do not want anything from them.
It is simply because I have been bullied by this lot that I cannot bear it any longer. I hope my Master will show me compassion. The Elder... [continued].
The Old Man said, "I will keep you for myself; it is simply that it would not look well on Elder Chang’s face.
Tomorrow I shall write a letter to him. When he sends a reply, I will take you in; then both houses will look well. Ji Gong said, "My Master sees it thus.
That evening, Ji Gong took temporary rest in the abbot’s quarters. The next morning, the Elder wrote [the letter].
The letter was delivered. A messenger was dispatched to Lingyin Monastery. At that time, Elder Chang was sitting in the abbot’s quarters.
The attendant announced, "A messenger from Jingci Monastery is here. The Elder directed him to come forward. The messenger presented the letter.
It is said:
The Bhikṣu Dehui, Abbot of Jingci Temple on Nanying Mountain, bows his head before the Dharma-seat of his senior brother, Master Chang.
As the morning dawns, the new bamboo shoots gradually grow and the green trees form shade. I respectfully wish that you may enjoy peace and well-being in your meditative practice.
May your pure merit increase tenfold. Sangdaoji arrived at a dilapidated temple on the upper mountain and said, "I have been appointed as the fundraiser for salt and vegetables.
When I was drunk, I gave my consent; now that I am sober, it is difficult to carry out. He hid himself in a side room, having no way to return and face the situation.
I respectfully submit this note, humbly hoping for your compassion. Please consider that this monk has long suffered from a chronic alcoholism;
if you would deign to look upon my humble face, I shall naturally deliver it tomorrow.
When Elder Chang saw this, he was greatly incensed and said, "Dowei received three prostrations from me, yet he could not raise even half a coin."

Upon seeing the Elder, he stepped forward and paid his respects. The Elder said, "Without informing me, you went out directly for half a year.
What kind of principle is that? Ji Gong replied, "I was merely wandering about idly. I hope the Elder will show me compassion. The Elder said, "But as for me—"
Instead of being spared ridicule, he was laughed at by everyone. Ji Gong said, "From now on, I shall never dare to act like this again.

Thereafter, Ji Gong devoted himself solely to sitting in meditation and reciting sutras. When the weather of the third month arrived, Ji Gong said to the Elder, "Since returning to the temple, I have never once gone out.
Now I wish to go outside; I come specifically to inform you, Elder, so that you may take note. The Elder...

The Old Man said, "Go now; you must return within only one or two days. Ji Gong replied, "I shall respectfully obey," and departed from the abbot’s quarters, heading straight for Wansong Ridge to arrive at the residence of Imperial Commissioner Mao.
He ordered the gatekeeper to announce his arrival. The Commissioner hurried out to welcome him, and they entered to sit.
After tea was served, the Commissioner said, "Since the Empress Dowager and you visited our temple together, it has already been—"
"It has been more than half a year. Lord Ji said, 'I have long been indebted to you, Excellency, for bringing this magnificent undertaking to completion.
It is because I recently thought of some wine that I have come to visit you. The Grand Marshal said, 'Sit down for a moment. Today, the gardeners dug up some bamboo shoots;
I shall present half to the court and keep half here. I have ordered them to be boiled so that you may taste the new season's produce. Lord Ji was greatly pleased."
"Delicious! I have already consumed more than half a bowl. Its flavor is truly exquisite. The Buddha’s words say:
"One cun or two cun, the officials have their share; one chi or two chi, the commoners may eat. If you, Monk, wish to eat, you must wait until the walls are woven.

We, your humble servants, have the great honor of tasting the new harvest while Your Reverence remains in the monastery—you would not see it even in a dream. I shall simply set aside a few [extra portions]..."
Ji Gong took a piece of meat, returned home, and offered it to the Elder. The Grand Marshal said, "This is the leftovers.
He then set aside another plate, wrapped it securely in lotus leaves, and Ji Gong took up the lotus-leaf parcel as a token of thanks and departed.
Along the way toward the main gate of Jingci Temple, the Head Seat asked, "What is in that parcel in your hand? Is it dog meat? Ji Gong replied, "No, it is not. He opened the parcel...
"Internal things—your dreams cannot even perceive them. The assembly asked, "What, then, is it?
Jigong stuffed his bundle and pushed it past them, saying, "Just smell this," and then went straight into the abbot’s quarters. The Elder asked, "How is it that you have returned so soon?
Jigong replied, "I went straight to the residence of Minister Mao; I was just about to taste some fresh delicacies."
"Brother, I have obtained a bundle of bamboo shoots. Let me offer some fresh ones to the Elder. The Elder said, "It is rare for you to find such things.
Ji Gong ordered an attendant to bring a tray. He untied the lotus-leaf wrapping and poured the contents onto the tray.
Holding it up before the Elder, the Elder ate two or three pieces and distributed some to each person. The assembly of monks all came forward to ask for bamboo shoots to eat.
The Elder said, "There are fixed portions; these have all been distributed.

Ji Gong said, "While I was in the residence of Grand Secretary Mao, I spoke of Chan principles and brought forth the bamboo shoots. You all merely concerned yourselves with eating them with your bare mouths.
The Elder asked, "What Chan principles did you speak? Ji Gong replied, "One cun, two cun—officials have their shares. One chi, two chi."
"The common people get to eat them; you, Master Monk, must wait until they have woven the walls [to eat].
The Elder said, “Truly marvelous! Truly marvelous! The assembly of monks said, “It would be well if you could solicit some for us to taste these new shoots.
Ji Gong said, “If the assembly of monks can take ‘new bamboo shoots’ as a theme and compose a poem, I shall go and solicit two loads. Thereupon, the Elder composed one.
A single verse says:
Bamboo shoots first emerge like the horns of a young calf; New bracken sprouts grow like the fists of small children.
Picking wild greens to cook fragrant rice— This is precisely the second month of Jiangnan.
Jigong said, "Not today, nor tomorrow; on the day after tomorrow, I shall give you two loads.
The Elder said, "These fresh bamboo shoots have only just sprouted; how can they be measured by the load? Jigong replied, "Do not concern yourself with that.
The following day, Jigong went straight to the residence of Grand Secretary Mao at Wansong Ridge. Upon arriving at the hall and sitting down, Jigong said, "Yesterday, I was honored by..."
[The Emperor] bestowed bamboo shoots. The Elder ate them, and the assembly of monks all sought some as well. I spoke of it all at once.

"Today I have come specifically to solicit alms for two loads," [the donor said]. The Grand Marshal said, "If more than ten days had passed and they had emerged in abundance, there would have been plenty.

The Grand Marshal said with delight, "Bring me the head of the memorial; I shall give you bamboo shoots. Ji Gong took up paper and brush and wrote in a single stroke:
"Brocade screens shattered like jade—truly suited for our alms-bowls; Powdered joints rising above the wall—already belong to another's breeze."
The moon is just right for dragging through the mud and digging it out; how could one bear to carry it back dripping with dew? Within the cauldron of salt and oil, it is roasted into gold;

"I, this mountain monk, have tasted it all; its flavor is fresh and sweet. May the donor alone enjoy it, and may their fortune and rank remain forever firm.
The Grand Marshal said with delight, "Today it has finally sprouted; let us let it grow for one night. Tomorrow morning we shall dig it up, and we shall surely obtain even more.
Ji Gong said, "Just so! Just so! That evening, the Grand Marshal invited Ji Gong to stay overnight at his residence.
The next morning, Ji Gong entered the bamboo grove with him. There they saw approximately five loads of bamboo shoots that had been excavated.
Five guards were assigned to carry them away. Ji Gong thanked the Grand Marshal and proceeded to Jingci Temple.
When the monks at the mountain gate saw Ji Gong approaching leading five loads of bamboo shoots, they hurriedly informed the Elder. Ji Gong said, "Bamboo shoots..."
He then vanished. "You all should contribute five hundred cash notes to repay the cost of the journey," he said. The Elder replied, "I have my own.
He then ordered his attendant to fetch five hundred cash notes and gave them to the five men who had delivered the bamboo shoots.

Fengzi said, "Do not look for him. Go and report that he is not here. The attendant reported this to Ji Gong. Ji Gong was greatly incensed;
he went straight to the West Hall room, but the Junior West Hall monk was also not there. He asked a novice for a brush.
He went down to the Cold Spring Pavilion and composed a regulated verse, saying:
For several hundred years, Lingyin Temple Has now been bolted shut by an iron ox.
Within its hooves lies a leak that cannot be cultivated; Its nostrils reach toward heaven, refusing to be pierced.
How can the eye of the Way compare to the blind eyes of a donkey? The temple gate is always like the barred gate of a prison.
Cold Spring has water, yet no gulls or egrets; it merely causes one’s name to remain in the world.
Having finished writing this, he handed it to an attendant boy and further inscribed it upon the plaster wall of the West Hall, saying:
A tiny hermitage with tiny windows, A tiny room with a tiny bed;
The young acolytes move about in small steps, Attending with careful devotion to the Junior Abbot.
Jigong bid farewell to the young attendant and returned to the temple. Now, as for Lingyin Temple, someone reported to the Elder: [Text continues...]

"The pine trees on both sides must be cut down. The Elder said, "What should we do? Jigong replied, "Elder, do not be alarmed. Wait for me to go see him.

The Abbot. Ji Gong stepped forward and paid his respects. The Governor said, "Are you indeed that Ji Dian? I have long heard that you are skilled at composing poetry.

Towering a hundred feet high, it reaches toward the heavens; In the past, it shared a long-standing friendship with mountain monks.

"The most sorrowful are the cranes that fly away at dawn, Returning at dusk to find their former nests no more.

At the child’s gate, he saw a placard pasted there; struck with alarm, he went inside and found Mistress Wang weeping by the coffin.
Mistress Wang said, "The old man and you have been close friends for some time. When his funeral takes place tomorrow, please come to see him off and assist with the cremation.

Jigong said, "If that is the case, let us go and sit upon the Long Bridge.

He led Shen Yi to the temple to meet the Elder. Master Ji said, "I have found a disciple here;
I hope the Elder will grant him his acceptance. The Elder then conferred the empowerment upon him by touching his head with his hand and changed his name to Shen Wanfa.
The following day after the meal, Ji Gong ordered Shen Wanfa to fetch some fire. Wanfa asked, "What will you do with the fire?
Ji Gong replied, "I am sitting idly today and wish to roast a few lice. Shortly thereafter, Wanfa brought over a basin of fire.
Ji Gong took off his *zhidu* (monastic robe) and held it over the fire to roast it; two lice emerged.
A louse emerged from his body. Ji Gong said, "Even lice have husbands and wives. I wish to bite them to death, yet I fear it would defile my mouth.
It would be better to burn them in the fire. He then placed the louse into the fire and recited these words:
Listen to my words, you lice; you must now take them to heart. Among the ranks of insects and ants, you dwell only where there is flesh and blood.
Refusing to be born in a pure place, you come to be born within my trousers. Not large, yet not small as a sesame seed, you have both husbands and wives, turning and twisting thus as you are born.
When will you be sated by sucking me? My body itself is not lacking for you, so how could you...
Be firm and resolute; turn toward this single hearth of fire. Do not give rise to fear or dread. Cast away this wriggling carcass and do not return by the path you came.
Aha! Amidst the blazing light, a single crackle erupts; in every moment it sinks into stillness, leaving no trace to be found.

once it is finished, return immediately. I went straight there. As the funeral rites were about to begin, Master Ji said, "I shall go along and guide them for them," and he recited these words:
The King of the Flour-Mashers possesses a most composed nature; he grinds beans by the hundreds of times and steams cakes by the thousands.
He consumes vast amounts of fragrant oil and burns tens of thousands of logs of wood.
Today, all shall be scattered and lost; his daily patrons can no longer be retained. Spirit!
The coffin has arrived; where shall it be placed?
*Ei!* A gust of eastern wind cannot blow it away; birds cry, flowers fall, and the waters flow empty.
On one side, the materials for the pyre are prepared. Proceeding to Fangjiaju to perform the cremation, Master Ji takes up a torch and says to the assembly:
Listen: Old Lady Wang gave me rice-flour soup to eat, Intending to send the Duke Wang to the Western Land;
Though the Western Land is eighty-four thousand li away, For now, he shall remain right here in Yuhang.
Having finished his thoughts, he saw a young man approach and bow before Wang Po; it was the neighbor of his daughter.

Because of this, she specifically asked a neighbor to announce the birth. When Old Lady Wang heard this, she was overjoyed, while everyone else was struck with amazement.
Jigong was surrounded by the crowd, so he leaped onto the table and performed a somersault, exposing his private parts.
The people burst into laughter, and while they were still laughing, Jigong went straight on his way.
He entered through the Qingdu Gate and came to the New Palace Bridge, where he went into Shen Pingzhai’s herbal medicine shop. The mistress of the house held Jigong in high esteem.
When the Duke saw Ji Gong, he hurriedly invited him inside. Once they were seated and the tea had been served, the Madam ordered wine to be prepared.
She placed a large bowl before Ji Gong; with one go, Ji Gong drank more than ten bowls.
He was already feeling intoxicated. The serving maid then brought out another bowl of spicy fish broth.
The Mistress said, "Have a few more bowls. Ji Gong drank another dozen or so bowls until he was thoroughly drunk.
He thanked the Mistress and, stumbling toward Qingbo Gate, fell down in one fell swoop. The gatekeepers and passersby surrounded him; among them was someone who recognized him.
De said, "This monk Jì of Jingci Temple is extremely skilled at composing poetry; he simply lacks decorum when drinking wine.

Originally, this was the body of one who had cultivated the four fruits of arhatship; now, feigning madness, he mingles with common folk.

The assembly of monks did not realize what was happening; they all spat upon him. Ji Gong could not stop himself and continued to shout until the third watch.

A single point of namelessness arises in hesitation; A thousand halls of a great mansion are all turned to dust.
