The Abbot said, "I have already repented and shall soon depart. Having said this, he vanished. The next morning, the Abbot's body was found to have completely disappeared. Master Ji sighed and said, "How could I have known that the Abbot was a ghost? It is truly as the saying goes: 'When the wise lead, the people follow. He then composed a verse: *The Abbot’s room was burned, yet no ashes remained;* *The ghost thanked us for our compassion, and ascended to heaven.* *If one wishes to avoid such a fate,* *One must practice the Way with utmost sincerity.* *Do not look down on those who are lowly;* *For the karmic retribution of the past is profound.* *Only by cultivating virtue and doing good* *Can one escape the cycle of birth and death.* He then ordered the laborers to sweep the site clean once more. From that time on, the monastery flourished even more than before. Master Ji said, "This is why we say: 'The wise are like a mirror; they reflect the truth. If one is not careful, one may fall into the same error as the Abbot. Thus, he urged everyone to be diligent in their practice. This story is recorded in the *Ji Gong Zhuan*. It serves as a warning to all practitioners: do not harbor arrogance or contempt for others, lest you suffer such consequences. One must always maintain a humble and compassionate heart. This is the true meaning of practicing the Way. May all beings take heed. End of story.
In a lifetime, there was neither profit nor fame; With shaven head and square robe, he walked freely on the Path.
Mindfulness arose solely from the heart; The mechanisms of Chan were all produced from the root of the tongue.
For hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, what is provisional is not provisional; For sixty-three years, what is real is not real.
"Now I am going into the Nameless Thicket; not a single thing shall remain at Nanping," said Master Ji.

"Elder, you have already departed for Mount Tiantai. For now, let the laborers gather some wood that has not been consumed by the fire and erect several thatched huts so the monks may have a place to stay. Master Ji then proceeded to the kitchen.
Seeing a large cauldron of hot water, he cried out loudly, "There is fine hot water here! Come and wash your faces.
I have a little song; let me sing it for you to dispel your boredom. He sang:
At Jingci Temple, the Buddha Hall and both corridors built by the Qian Wang were completely burned down. Only two *vajrapāṇi* remained;

even the Buddha was vexed and emitted a jade-white light from his brow. It was like a military training ground in mid-air, yet there was still a bit of profit—not losing one's capital for a pot of cold water exchanged for a pot of hot broth.
The assembly of monks laughed together, saying, "You have gone mad. "The two *jian-si* (administrative stewards) have been placed in stocks at the Long Bridge;
you must rescue them! Ji Gong walked for a while until he reached the Long Bridge, where he saw the two *jian-si* there in stocks. Ji Gong said:
The two of you have poked your heads out from within the boards; it is like having a lantern atop a cannon mounted on a shelf.
The Abbot said, "Brother, instead of saving us, you come to mock us. Ji Gong replied, "I will save you! I will save you!
He went straight to the residence of Grand Secretary Mao. The Grand Secretary received him and cried out, "Fire! Fire! Ji Gong said, "It cannot be said—"

Agreed. Once the two men were seated, the Grand Marshal immediately arranged for wine. They drank until they were half-intoxicated, at which point Ji Gong said, "I am deeply grateful to you, Grand Marshal, for allowing me to drink here.
However, our two superintendents are currently imprisoned in stocks at the Long Bridge; I hope you will rescue them. The Grand Marshal replied, "It is no trouble at all;
I shall write a letter to take to Governor Zhao and have him release them immediately. The next morning...
Jigong said to the Grand Marshal, "Let us go to the fire site and see. Upon reaching the temple gate, they saw two superintendents returning.
The monks were overjoyed and asked how they had managed to secure their release.
The superintendents replied that it was thanks to Jigong’s request to Grand Marshal Mao, who instructed Governor Zhao to set them free. Consequently, everyone was released.
The monks all thanked Jigong. The head seat said, "Who could possibly serve as the abbot of this temple?
Jigong replied, "It must be the elder Song Shaolin from Baoben Temple in Puzhou; he would be suitable.
The prior said, "That elder is indeed excellent, but his age is advanced. How could he ever be willing to come? Jigong said, "If you want him to come, he will come."
"You must buy wine to invite me," he said. The Prior replied, "This is a matter for the entire community. At present we have no money; how could we afford to buy wine to invite you?
I shall write a letter myself and send someone to invite you. Ji Gong said, "If you cannot get him to come, do not blame me for laughing.
He then departed toward the residence of the Grand Minister (Taewei). The monks of the temple prepared a formal letter and sent it off.
The messenger was sent to Baoshou Temple in Puzhou to see the Elder and present the letter. The Elder said, "I am advanced in years;
how could I possibly go? The messenger pleaded with him repeatedly, but the Elder replied, "It is not for his sake."
"It is truly difficult to take action. Let the guest prefect be informed; once the meal is finished, send a messenger to offer our thanks.
Upon returning to our own temple, we shall recount the previous events in full detail. The Head Seat said, "We must have Master Ji write a letter; then we shall send another messenger again."
The assembly of monks said, "It is so," and immediately purchased a jar of wine and invited Master Ji. In a single session, he drank more than ten bowls.
Master Ji asked, "When you invited the Elder of Shaolin the other day, what did he say when you returned with his message?
The Head Monk replied, "The other day we went there for nothing. Today I have come specifically to ask you to write a letter. Master Ji then composed it instantly.

He sealed it securely and handed it to the messenger, who set out on his journey. Upon arriving at Puzhou, he presented himself before the Elder, saying, "Venerable Monk, you sent me away with instructions yesterday;
why have you come back? The messenger replied, "The Secretary Ji has a letter here which I present to you.
The Elder tore it open, looked at it, and was greatly pleased. The letter read: [The letter follows.]
The semblance Dharma is gradually decaying, and the ancestral style has grown faint. People come and go, yet none truly let go; they wander aimlessly, each seeking their own fragrance.
We must rely upon a man of true substance. Today, by the public consensus of all, we respectfully honor the Great Monk of Shaolin:
his conduct illuminates the sages of old, and his virtue protects future generations. He wields the hammer and chisel of the Buddha’s teachings and unfolds the [monastic]...
You, whose nostrils are as those of a man, do not let yourself be shamed by the expectations of the myriad mountains; do not decline the toil of a single stream.
Before Mount Huiri, may you discern the verse that breaks through the precipice; at the side of Nanping Mountain, may you fully realize the luster of the spiritual jade.
Out of compassion for human sentiment, do not weary yourself with the labor of being led by the nose.
The Elder of Shaolin, having finished reading it, said, "This time I must go and make the journey. He immediately ordered the drums to be beaten and the bells struck to assemble the great assembly.
He selected a man of virtuous conduct to serve as the abbot of the temple, hung up the notice board, and instructed the messenger to return first.
He told the Secretary Jiji not to leave, while he himself packed his belongings, intending to remain within this very month.
He arrived immediately and sent word of his departure, first returning to his own temple to inform them. The assembly of monks was greatly delighted and wished to keep Master Ji in the monastery.
Master Ji said, "If I do not go out, how shall I get wine to drink? He set off straight away, crying out for them to stop him, but they could not detain him.
The Administrative Rector said, "If we keep him here, how will we have the money to buy wine every day?
Yet, if we do not keep him, the Elder will be displeased. The Head Seat said, "It is easy. I have a large empty jar kept at a neighbor's house.
We shall take it there, fill it with lake water, and seal the mouth of the jar. We will treat it as wine purchased on credit, and only open it when the Elder arrives."
This may be taken as a laugh. The Abbot’s Assistant said, “That is best. He then went to fetch Ji Gong back. The Head Seat said, “Ji Gong, we have no money.
Let us buy a fine jar of wine on credit. You must look after it and wait until the Elder arrives before opening it.”
Jigong said, "It will do no harm; you may buy it on credit. In a moment, two masons carried the wine to Jigong’s presence.
Jigong said, "Open it and let us taste it. The Head Seat said, "If one opens newly fired clay jars, they must vent their heat.
Jigong said, "That is true," and then he tipped the jar slightly, saying, "This shall suffice for my intoxication. He then gave the order.
The fire-worker carried it and placed it beneath a thatched hut. After several days had passed, someone reported that the Elder was arriving.
The assembly of monks all went out a long way to welcome the Elder of Shaolin to the temple. Once the monks had finished paying their respects to the Elder, they proceeded to converse with Jigong.
Jigong said, "Do not be alarmed; let us first attend to the matter at hand," and then struck a brick with [his staff].
He uncovered his head; smelling only the scent of water, he became greatly enraged and smashed the jar with one blow, cursing, "This pack of shaven-headed donkeys!
They have clearly been playing tricks on me! When the Elder of Shaolin heard this, he asked, "What is being done?
The attendant replied, "Jigong wanted to drink wine and made a scene. The Elder said, "If Jigong wants to drink wine, buy two bottles at random and invite him."
Suddenly, Ji Gong came before the Elder and said, "How can these shaven-headed donkeys keep playing tricks on me?
The Elder replied, "Do not treat them with such familiarity. I shall buy wine myself to entertain you.
Ji Gong said, "I have not yet been welcomed by you, Elder; what logic is there in having you buy wine to invite me? After a short while...
The wine arrived. Ji Gong drank it. The Elder said, "I have only recently arrived and am not familiar with this monastery.
Has a fundraising notice ever been posted regarding the reconstruction after the fire? Ji Gong replied, "This lot of shaven-headed brutes each attends to their own domestic affairs;
they do not care for the essential business. The Elder said, "In that case, you shall write it for me today. He then ordered his attendant to fetch the four treasures of the study.
"Come," said Jigong, as he took up his brush and completed the work at once, not adding a single stroke.
He said: "I humbly submit: Zhurong has raised the provocation, casting light upon ten thousand acres of calm lake;
Fengbo lends his aid, sweeping away five hundred great halls. Fiery embers fly like stars across the distant heavens; clamorous dust locks the layered peaks in a mist."
Each carrying their cloud-tipped staff, they set out together in ox-carts. The former gold and azure have all turned to soot;
who among those passing the gate does not feel their heart tremble? Even with eyes closed, one still suspects it is a dream.
Reflecting deeply, even an Arhat cannot remain sitting coldly; he raises the light of the jade-hair. How pitiful that even the Teacher, the Tamer of Men, has also been thoroughly scorched.
The golden flower seat has been lost, yet though many ages have passed, the hearts of men remain unsatiated. The bells and drums sound again as a warning from the void;
the incense and lamps are once more offered in honor of the former Emperor. Within the city of Vaiśālī, there have always been great donors;
in the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden, a monastery (*ārāma*) can be completed in a matter of days. Indestructible like a diamond, the iron stupa serves as witness.
The Elder looked upon this with great joy and instructed his attendant to hang the proclamation at the mountain gate.
Those who came to view it were as numerous as ants. After several days had passed, Ji Gong said, "I have already transformed it. Tomorrow the master of the arts will arrive.

The following morning, indeed, the Imperial Court dispatched a Grand Marshal to deliver thirty thousand strings of precious paper, stating that he had dreamed of a golden-bodied Arhat soliciting funds during the night.

For this reason, I have brought this great undertaking to completion. Once the assembly of elder monks had finished expressing their gratitude, the treasury office collected thirty thousand strings of cash.
After the midday meal, the Grand Marshal escorted [the monks] out through the mountain gate. A date was chosen for the commencement of construction.

Officials from various prefectures, counties, and districts, as well as wealthy patrons, all made offerings. Within less than two years, the halls, pavilions, corridors, and dwellings were all fully completed.
One day, Ji Gong visited Leifeng Pagoda during his leisure time. Looking toward Elder Chang, the elder said, "Ji Gong, you have been hard at work supervising the construction for some time now;
today I shall share a cup with you. Ji Gong replied, "I am deeply grateful, Elder.
He then instructed his attendant to set out wine beneath the Shuiyun Pavilion. By that time, Ji Gong was already intoxicated and said, "I have troubled you enough."
He wrote a poem in thanks, which read:
The misty waves stretch far, meeting the heavens; In this place where the dust of the world is sparse, I have built a cottage of three rafters.
I do not worry that the scenery will vanish by tomorrow morning, But only fear that the waters and clouds may join together at evening.
White egrets fly beside the Azure Ink Mountains; Fishermen’s boats moor by the green willow embankments.
Tranquil and leisurely, this place is truly fit for joy— Half human world, half realm of immortals.
Having finished writing, he drank more wine. Just then, a fire-worker arrived and said, "The Elder has an invitation. Ji Gong hurriedly rose.
Having thanked him, he returned to the monastery and entered the abbot’s quarters. The Elder asked, "Where have you been?
Jigong replied, "I was wandering idly and arrived at Elder Chang’s temple; they invited me there for a drink. The Elder said, "I have wine here specifically for you.
After a short while, the attendant brought the wine, and Jigong drank ten or more bowls until he was intoxicated.

The Master said, "In my mouth, I have always said that our main temple owes much to the Elder acting as its presiding authority. I, too, have applied my mind, and thus it has been brought to this state.
Only the murals on the two corridors remain unfinished; my heart cannot rest at ease. The Elder replied, "If that is the case," and so forth.

"Please finish this for me; it would be well," [the Elder] said. Ji Gong replied, "I have completed my fundraising in all other places, but only the newly appointed Magistrate Wang of Lin’an Prefecture has not yet been solicited.
The Elder said, "I have heard that when this official was still an unexamined candidate, he went to a temple to offer alms.
He was deceived by the monks and managed to escape. He was often angry about this and inscribed on the wall: 'When encountering the guest-master...'"

He was like a tortoise; when he encountered the fast-day, his neck would extend like that of a goose. To this day, he harbors resentment toward the Master. "Do not try to convert him," [the monks] said.
Ji Gong replied, "It matters not. I am determined to convert him. The assembly of monks could not dissuade him, so Ji Gong left the monastery and went straight to the front of the prefectural office.
Anfu was standing on Xuanhua Bridge. While he was in the hall, he saw a monk on the bridge peering about suspiciously.

He instructed his attendants to quietly bring him inside. When the four attendants reached the bridge, they seized him by the hair and pushed Ji Gong into the hall to kneel. Anfu said, "This shaven-headed donkey!"
"How dare you be so audacious? Ji Gong said. "I am the monk Jidian, the registrar of Jingci Temple.
We share a karmic connection that only you, Excellency, can understand; I have come specifically to deliberate with you. Hearing this, Anfu ordered the beating to cease.
"If you speak well," Ji Gong continued, "I shall forgive you for the blows already struck. If you speak poorly, you shall receive double the punishment."
The Duke said, "In the past, when the Layman Dongpo, Qin Shaoyou, Huang鲁直 (Huang Tingjian),
and Chan Master Foyin— these four— were drinking together, Dongpo proposed a toast requiring two names of ancient poets for the same object,
followed by two lines of verse. Everyone was worried for Ji Gong, but Ji Gong remained calm and composed, saying, 'Listen, my lord.'"
Su Dongpo said: "The brush hairs fall to the ground without a sound; looking up, I see Guan Zhong. Guan Zhong asks Bao Shu:
'For what reason do you not plant bamboo? Bao Shu replies: 'I need only two or three stalks; the pure breeze will naturally suffice.'"
Qin Shaoyou said: "When snowflakes fall to the ground, they make no sound; raising one's head, one sees Bai Qi. Bai Qi asked Lian Po:
'For what reason do you not raise geese? Lian Po replied: 'White feathers float upon the green water; red palms stir the clear waves.'"
Huang鲁直 (Lu-zhi) said: "When the woodworm’s shavings fall to the ground, they make no sound. Raising one's head, one sees Confucius. Confucius asks Yan Hui:
'For what reason do you not plant plum trees? Yan Hui replies: 'Deep within the snows of the village ahead, last night a single branch has blossomed.'"
Foyin said, "The heavenly flowers fall to the ground without a sound; lift your head and you see Amitābha. Amitābha asked Vimalakīrti, "Why do you speak so much?
Vimalakīrti replied, "When meeting a guest, his head is like a turtle; when encountering a vegetarian feast, his neck is like a goose."
The Pacifier (Anfu) heard this and laughed heartily. He invited Ji Gong into the rear hall; once they were seated and the tea had been served, he ordered that wine be prepared.

With the Pacifier attending as host, Ji Gong said, "Our temple has suffered from wind and fire. Now that we have received offerings from patrons from all directions, we are rebuilding it entirely anew.
However, only the wall-filling work for the two corridors remains unfinished. We specifically request that you, Excellency, generously grant us your assistance. The Pacifier... [consented].
The Governor said, "I have not been in office for long; how could I have any offerings to give? Ji Gong replied, "If you can resolve to do so, do not worry about lacking cash.
He continued, "The Buddha’s words say: 'What is given in the light will come back in the dark. The Governor said, "Since that is so, I shall find a way.
As it was already late, the Governor invited Ji Gong to stay the night. The next morning, he immediately prepared three thousand strings of his official stipend.
The official dispatched men to escort him away. Ji Gong went straight to Jingci Temple, where the abbot and the assembly of monks received him; they all cheered and applauded.
The administrative office (Kusi) took charge of the cash and prepared a vegetarian feast to await the return of the messengers to the prefecture.

Meanwhile, they invited an artist to paint a portrait. Ji Gong spent several days in the temple looking at the paintings; suddenly, thinking of some wine to drink, he walked out through the Nine Li Bridge.
In Song, there was a household that had begun construction on a three-bay hall and requested two lines of Buddhist verse to be inscribed upon the ridgepole.

Master Ji said, "Bring some wine. After a short while, the wine arrived. Master Ji took one seat and drank twelve or thirteen bowls. He then hurriedly told the craftsmen to begin their work together and lift the ridgepole.
Master Ji stood upon a stool and recited: "Three bays wide, nine spans deep; The ridgepole is raised, the rafters are set. May the family live long and prosper; May the ancestors rest in peace."
Today we ascend the red beams; may we escape the loss of a thousand mouths. The wife dies before her husband; the son perishes ahead of his father.
When the master of the house heard this, he was displeased in his heart. Who would have thought that Ji Gong’s words were all in accord with reason? (Title)

He finished and left the gate. Passing by a wonton shop, the proprietor recognized Ji Gong and invited him inside. He requested that Ji Gong eat some wontons; after Ji Gong had eaten them, he took the wontons as his theme and borrowed a brush to write upon the wall: The Wonton Shop By the Great Monk Ji Gong A bowl of steaming hot wontons, Fresh meat and fine vegetables within. When the hungry man eats them, they are most delicious; When the poor man eats them, they are most satisfying. If you wish to know their price, It is but three cash per bowl. The proprietor read this and was filled with admiration. He then asked, "Great Monk, where are you going? Ji Gong replied, "I am going to the Temple of the Five Hundred Arhats. The proprietor said, "Great Monk, please stay for a while and let me prepare some tea. Ji Gong accepted the invitation and sat down.

As they were about to drink the tea, the proprietor suddenly saw that the writing on the wall had vanished. Startled, he looked around and saw that the Great Monk had already departed. The proprietor sighed in regret, saying, "How extraordinary! How could such a thing happen? He then went home and told his wife what had occurred. His wife said, "This is surely the handiwork of the Great Monk. The proprietor then went back to the wall and found the verse still there, exactly as it had been written before. He realized that the Great Monk’s supernatural powers were truly inconceivable. From that day forward, the reputation of the Wonton Shop spread far and wide. People from all quarters came to eat, and the business flourished. It is said that even today, the verse remains on the wall. It is truly a wonder. One must not fail to visit this place. It is located at the corner of the street near the Temple of the Five Hundred Arhats. Those who pass by should not forget to look. (To be continued)
Encompassing all phenomena, his nature is coarse and bold; with purity as his root, he performs prostrations and joins his palms.
His entire body is seamless, without a single gap. When he maintains his composure, he performs somersaults within the cauldron of boiling water, swallowing both horizontally and vertically;
when he cannot maintain it, he runs east and west. This is precisely when this mountain monk chews it to pieces: muddy oxen fill the ground, snorting and roaring.
"Hou! Having finished writing, suddenly a man fell by the road and died at the entrance of the gate. The crowd was in a state of commotion and clamor.
When the innkeeper saw this, he said in a panic, "This headless corpse—what is to be done? Ji Gong replied, "It is of no matter. I..."
"I shall do you a good deed," he said, and then addressed the corpse with this verse:
"O dead man, in what village do you dwell? For what illness have you perished on the street?
I now point out a path for you: Go forward and rest in peace in a quiet place."
Just then, the corpse scrambled up and ran straight toward the foot of the ridge, where it died.
The innkeeper and his neighbors were filled with great joy. Meanwhile, Ji Gong took a path back to the temple;
he saw clouds gathering on all sides and a man rushing to take cover from the rain, with a banner stuck in his hair. Ji Gong asked, "What is your honorable surname? Afterward—
A man named Huang was selling rice in Zhugan Lane. He had only one mother, who was eighty years old.
Master Ji asked him, "Have you been filial toward her in your daily life? The man replied, "How could I not be filial toward my own biological parents?
Master Ji said, "The karma of your past lives is heavy; I shall save you. Follow me to the abbot’s quarters, where we will set out [the offerings]."
He lowered the table and wrapped himself in his *kāṣāya*. He had the junior monks hide beneath the table, while Ji Gong sat cross-legged upon it. He then recited:
"You young man, you young man! You have suddenly incurred the wrath of Heaven. For the evil karma of your past life, you now possess this pale body.
I, an old monk, shall save you. Return and serve your mother; commit no evil deeds so that calamity may be avoided.
He saw only a single old pine tree that had been smashed to pieces. The young man rose, offered his thanks, and departed. — Jigong.
One day he left the temple and arrived at the former Yangsi, in front of a nunnery.

The nuns there had long heard people say that Ji Gong was at Lingyin Temple soliciting donations to refurbish the Buddha statue, yet spent his days drinking wine and causing the monks to lodge complaints against him for being excessively drunk.
He spat upon the Buddha’s head. The next day, the three great Buddhas were found to be cast of pure gold; they were truly living Buddhas.
Because he wished to exchange them for the bronze bell, he requested that Master Jigong write a formal petition on his behalf.

Just as he was about to arrive, Master Men said, "The Abbot has specifically sent me to invite you. Master Jigong replied, "It is most opportune that I have come. Entering the inner quarters, he saw the Abbot.
Once the abbot was seated, Ji Gong said, "If you wish to invite me, you must simply get me drunk and then stop.
The abbot replied, "We nuns do not usually use wine. Upon hearing this, Ji Gong started to leave. The abbot said, "You are far too impatient; please sit for a moment."

After a short while, wine and delicacies were laid out. Ji Gong took his seat, consumed over twenty bowls of wine, and said, "Now it is settled. What do you wish to have done? The Abbot replied, "Our temple originally possessed an iron mirror, but we now intend to cast a bronze bell. We have come specifically to trouble you to write the draft for our petition. Ji Gong passed him the paper and brush and immediately wrote:

"May the Great Deity of the Iron Mirror, Who has long guarded the temple grounds, Now manifest his divine power to assist us. We shall melt down the mirror to cast a new bell; May you grant us your protection and blessings. Ji Gong finished writing and handed it back.

The Abbot thanked him profusely. Ji Gong then rose and departed. The Abbot took the draft, went to the temple office, and had the monks prepare the formal petition. He then sent a messenger to deliver it to the local magistrate. The magistrate read the draft and was greatly pleased, granting the request immediately. Consequently, the iron mirror was melted down and a magnificent bronze bell was cast. The sound of the bell resounded throughout the region, bringing peace and prosperity to all. Thus ended the tale of the casting of the bronze bell.
The nun was casting a bell; she had iron but no copper. "If you wish to complete it," [she said]. After Lián Sōng and Zhì Sōng finished writing [the inscription], they departed without taking leave.
When the head of the monastery saw this, he was displeased. Later, it was said that Imperial Protector Wang’s funeral procession arrived at Hupao Temple for burial.
There were two attendants from the Ministry of Rites (Shàirén): one named Lián Sōng and the other named Zhì Sōng; the elder brother—
The second younger brother also came to see the funeral procession. While walking idly, he entered a nunnery and saw a slip of paper on a table;
inside were the four characters "Lian Song Zhi Song. Greatly startled, he asked, "Who wrote this? The abbess replied:
Ji Fengzi said, "Lian Song, he is truly a living Buddha; he has already written the names of the two of us in advance.
Lian Song continued, "Since this is so, we brothers shall complete this bronze bell with all our might. Thereupon, the Abbot rose and expressed his gratitude.
He then prepared the vegetarian feast and waited for the two men to finish and return. On the following day, the two men completed their work with great diligence.
Now, as for Ji Gong returning to the temple, there was an old man who brought a piece of incense and sought out the Secretary Ji; he went straight into the Cloud Hall.

Jigong was seen sleeping. Hearing the sound of footsteps, he opened his eyes and saw the old man reaching into his chest and pulling out a piece of incense, which he then proffered toward Jigong while bowing.
He said, "I, your humble servant, have come specifically to trouble you, Master, to perform the cremation for my daughter.
Jigong asked, "Who is there? The old man replied, "I am the one who..."
At Jiansheng Street, the father of Lan Yueying, the head of the guild, approached him, saying: "Alas, my daughter has fallen ill and passed away.
Her funeral procession departs tomorrow, and today I have specifically invited the Master to perform the cremation rites. Ji Gong consented.
The following day, he directly sought out a small boat and crossed to Shiyuan Bridge. Upon reaching the shore, he saw that all those attending the funeral procession were...
Jigong arrived, following the coffin to the front of Jinniu Temple. Jigong said, "Old man, you want me to set fire to this; give me several strings of cash.
The old man replied, "I have one hundred strings of cash here. Jigong said, "There is no need for so much.
I only want five strings of cash to buy two bottles of wine. After I have drunk them, then..."
He extinguished the fire. In a short while, the wine arrived. Master Ji drank it and, holding a torch in his hand, recited:
"Deeply locked within the green window, painted eyebrows; Who knows of these myriad moods and thousandfold charms?

This scene and this moment, the person has departed; In vain I face the solitary phoenix as it flies alone. "Head of the Blue Quarter! Head of the Blue Quarter! Your character is like that of the plum blossom."
Her nature is gentle and mild; she makes her living within the mandarin duck curtains and finds her livelihood amidst the brocade clusters.
She removes the stone man’s cap and casts off the diamond sandals; using the rope of affection, she binds the unfeeling one.
The arrows of the five desires have been shot deep into the marrow of your bones; only when the lapis lazuli bottle is shattered will you finally realize that it was all but empty flowers.

Years of elegant refinement within the inner chambers have all become but falling petals and flowing water. For your sake, I, this mountain monk, shall strip away your bones and wash out your entrails.
"Eh! Having swept away the scent of a hundred years of rouge and powder, my entire body now naturally exudes fragrance.
After finishing his meal, Ji Gong suddenly thought of Zhang Gong, who lived on Feilai Peak. He went to look for him;
upon seeing Zhang Gong, he found Mistress Zhang coming out from inside, saying, "Ji Gong, you have come back at last! My dear husband!"
Last July, I suffered from dysentery and nearly died. Master Ji said, "I have been constantly worried about you all.
Zhang Po then prepared wine and delicacies, which Master Ji ate to his heart's content. He remarked, "I have troubled you enough;
tomorrow I shall be the host and invite you. You may come to find me at the crossroads in front of the East Garden."
Jigong offered his thanks and left the gate to return to the temple. As for Zhang Gong, on the following day he went straight to the front of the garden;
not seeing Jigong there and being hungry once more, he had no choice but to buy some noodles to eat. Upon leaving, he sought out the eastern quarter of the city.
Just as he entered, he looked up and saw a meat sausage hanging from a short pillar. Zhang Gong then untied it.
He tucked his sash at the waist and went straight home. Upon looking, they found ten ingots of white silver; the three of them were all struck dumb with astonishment.
